title: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
desc: Combines coding and broader evidence to separate whole-job productivity, experience effects, equalization and durable learning.

kps.k: AI can improve knowledge-work performance, but task-level gains do not establish whole-job productivity or worker replacement.
kps.d: The cluster tests the proposition that AI changes the cost, quality and distribution of skilled work rather than producing a uniform productivity uplift. Noy and Zhang’s March 2023 writing experiment reports completion time falling by 0.8 standard deviations and quality rising by 0.4. The Copilot workplace trials, covering 4,867 developers, estimate 26.08% more weekly pull requests among users (SE: 10.3%), using randomized access as an instrument for usage. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond’s November 2023 customer-support working paper reports 14% more issues resolved per hour. These measure different outcomes under human assistance; they are not interchangeable estimates of time savings, economic value or autonomous capability. Reviews that cite these experiments add interpretations, not independent replications.

qs.q: Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raises average productivity: time taken       decreases by 0.8 SDs and output quality rises by 0.4 SDs.
qs.a: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 14% on average, including a 34% improvement for novice and low-skilled workers but with minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.
qs.a: Generative AI at Work · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Contrasting coding results make task context and measurement central to the debate.
kps.d: The 95-programmer Copilot experiment reports 55.8% faster completion of a standardized JavaScript task. By contrast, METR’s February–June 2025 randomized trial finds 19% longer completion times across 246 predefined tasks undertaken by 16 experienced developers in familiar, mature repositories. METR identifies repository familiarity, size and maturity as plausible contributors, while allowing gains in other settings. The BCG experiments frame this heterogeneity as an uneven capability frontier: apparently similar professional tasks can differ in suitability for AI. Output counts can also rise through smaller pull requests or more verbose code without equivalent useful-work gains. Neither positive laboratory results nor the METR slowdown establishes a universal effect.

qs.q: The performance difference between treated and control groups are statistically and practi- cally significant: the treated group completed the task 55.8% faster (95% confidence interval:  21-89%).
qs.a: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot · Legal-tech vendor · 2023

qs.q: We find that when developers use AI tools, they implement issues in 19% more time on average (Figure 1), and nearly all quantiles of observed implementation time see AI-allowed issues taking longer (Figure 5).
qs.a: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Evidence that AI narrows performance gaps coexists with evidence that experienced or AI-skilled users capture more value.
kps.d: Writing and customer-support studies concentrate gains among weaker or less-experienced workers; the latter reports a 34% improvement for novice and low-skilled agents. An education-group experiment reduces the performance gap from 0.548 to 0.139 standard deviations, without claiming equal underlying abilities. Microsoft developer subgroup results point in the same direction, but differences are typically not statistically significant. Conversely, Daniotti and colleagues associate AI use with greater commit output and exploration mainly among experienced developers, despite higher usage among newcomers; their observational design does not establish causality. Anand and Idan identify AI Interaction Competence—eliciting, filtering and verifying output—as a predictor of gains. These findings distinguish experience, education, baseline performance and interaction competence rather than treating them as one skill measure.

qs.q: In the control group without AI, higher-education participants outperform lower-education participants by 0.548 standard deviations; with AI, this gap falls to 0.139 standard deviations, closing about three- quarters of the initial gap.
qs.a: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment · Academia · 2026

qs.q: For all three outcome measures, the effects on productivity are stronger for short-tenure/junior/less productive developers, though the difference is typically not statistically significant.
qs.a: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Assisted performance and durable skill formation can diverge.
kps.d: Generative AI at Work offers suggestive learning evidence: productivity remains above pre-AI levels during outages, particularly after greater exposure. The education experiment finds modest immediate unassisted carryover among lower-education participants, but explicitly does not treat its follow-up as a general skill-formation test. In contrast, How AI Impacts Skill Formation reports 17% lower evaluation scores after learning an unfamiliar Python library with AI, without a statistically significant speed gain. Its evidence covers a single chat-based task over one hour, not long-term workplace deskilling. Conceptual questioning and active engagement correlate with stronger learning across these studies, but those usage patterns were not separately randomized. The prospective concern is that shortcuts during learning could weaken the expertise later needed to verify AI output; long-run polarization remains a modeling prediction.

qs.q: Using data on software outages—periods in which the AI software fails to provide any suggestions—we show that workers see productivity gains relative to their pre-AI baseline even when recommendations are unavailable.
qs.a: Generative AI at Work · Academia · 2025

qs.q: We find that using AI assistance to complete tasks that involve this new library resulted in a reduction in the evaluation score by 17% or two grade points (Cohen’s d = 0.738, p = 0.010).
qs.a: How AI Impacts Skill Formation · Academia · 2026

kps.k: AI can redistribute tasks and some collaborative functions without eliminating human contribution.
kps.d: Noy and Zhang interpret writing gains mainly as substitution for effort, shifting work from drafting toward ideas and editing. Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs instead emphasizes complementary automation and augmentation: faster drafts alongside continued expertise and judgment. Generative AI and the Nature of Work links free Copilot eligibility to a 5.4-percentage-point increase in coding’s activity share and a 10-point reduction in project management’s share, with fewer collaborators and more exploration; these are activity shares, not hours saved. At P&G, AI-assisted individuals and teams improve by 0.37 and 0.39 standard deviations over unaided individuals. The authors infer substitution for certain teamwork functions, not wholesale replacement or statistical equivalence between conditions, and find evidence of iterative human shaping of outputs.

qs.q: ChatGPT mostly substitutes for worker effort rather than complementing       worker skills, and restructures tasks towards idea-generation and editing and away from       rough-drafting.
qs.a: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2023

qs.q: In all three instances, AI tools supplemented expertise rather than displaced experts.
qs.a: Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Adoption, preference and perceived savings are not substitutes for measured net benefits.
kps.d: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI reports that 23% of employed US respondents used AI at work in the previous week in late 2024, but only 9% used it every workday; estimated use covered 1–5% of work hours. METR participants still perceived a 20% time reduction after experiencing measured slowdown. Its later design update reports that 30–50% of surveyed developers withheld some tasks because they did not want to perform them without AI. The researchers infer downward selection bias, but preferences do not reveal gains on missing tasks. Meanwhile, low uptake and short treatment contrasts weaken precision in the Copilot workplace trials. Practical evaluation therefore needs actual usage, end-to-end time, useful output and quality—not access, acceptance rates or self-reports alone.

qs.q: 23 percent of employed respondents had used generative AI for work at least once in the previous week, and 9 percent used it every work day.
qs.a: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI · Academia · 2025

qs.q: After study participation, developers estimate that allowing AI reduced completion time by 20%.
qs.a: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Training, workflow design and verification condition deployment value, including in legal work.
kps.d: Training for Technology reports nearly one fine grade higher scores after targeted instruction than with LLM access alone; the access-only score decline was small and statistically insignificant. Anand and Idan report that conceptual scaffolding and training reduce performance dispersion without lowering mean performance. The Codex study interprets differences across user groups as evidence that permissions, system access, skills and review processes matter, rather than proving any organizational practice causes gains. Quality remains a separate question: early coding experiments did not assess it, while the open-source eligibility study reports fewer critical vulnerabilities within its measured setting. Legal reviews here mainly recount non-legal experiments, and Courts of Tomorrow supplies no quantified judicial outcomes. They therefore motivate application-specific testing rather than establish transferable legal-sector productivity gains.

qs.q: Compared to participants who only had access to an LLM, participants who received the intervention reported substantially higher rates of GenAI usage and achieved, on average, scores that were better by nearly one fine grade.
qs.a: Training for Technology: Adoption and Productive Use of Generative AI in Legal Analysis · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Our study complements this literature by providing controlled, causal micro-evidence: it isolates how differences in AIC levels shape productivity outcomes and demonstrates that lightweight process interventions—conceptual scaffolding and training—reduce variance without lowering mean performance.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Productivity gains for novices do not imply stronger entry-level employment; observed labor-market evidence remains contested.
kps.d: The US résumé and job-posting study reports reduced junior employment at adopting firms during 2023–2025, driven by slower hiring rather than separations, with senior employment unaffected. Its integrator-job-posting measure misses informal adoption and cannot establish aggregate effects. The Upwork study reports short-term declines of 2% in jobs and 5.2% in monthly earnings following ChatGPT’s release, without evidence that higher worker quality protects employment. Conversely, Still Waters, Rapid Currents links adoption surveys to administrative records and finds stable wages and hours alongside reorganization; adopting firms do not drive the employment declines it examines. The August 2026 Canaries revision explicitly labels its patterns descriptive rather than causal and flags pre-existing trends and dataset differences. These findings concern different populations, adoption measures and horizons, not one settled displacement estimate.

qs.q: By focusing not only on overall labor demand but on within- firm seniority composition, we provide evidence that GenAI-adopting firms reduce junior employment while leaving senior employment unaffected.
qs.a: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Résumé and Job Posting Data · Academia · 2025

qs.q: The release of ChatGPT leads to a 2% drop in the number of jobs on the platform, and a 5.2% drop in monthly earnings.
qs.a: The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Aggregate growth and distributional claims depend on assumptions beyond the experiments.
kps.d: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI adopts a conditional 27% task-level labor-cost-saving baseline, treating speed as savings, setting aside mixed quality effects and excluding the narrow programming task from its baseline. Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity projects 6.9% aggregate productivity growth over the next decade after allowing model improvement and updating inference costs; this is a forecast, not an observed translation or economy-wide outcome. Adoption-survey estimates likewise model potential productivity from reported savings. Whether workers gain depends on demand expansion, task substitution, organizational adjustment and who captures value. Generative AI at Work adds a compensation question: top performers supply training examples but receive few direct productivity gains. The practical implication is to track quality, learning, hiring, earnings and distribution alongside throughput rather than infer welfare from task performance alone.

qs.q: Under these assumptions, the average labor cost savings are 27% (= 0.27).
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: These changes leads to a significantly higher productivity estimate of around a magnitude higher than in Acemoglu (2024) with an estimate 6.9% productivity growth.
qs.a: Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Translation · Academia · 2024

vlens.an:
Across this curated set, academic and research sources accept the proposition that AI-assisted task performance cannot be treated as evidence of uniform whole-job productivity, worker replacement or durable skill growth. Their common rationale is methodological: outcomes depend on task context, user experience and interaction competence, institutional setting, adoption intensity, workflow design, verification, and the measure used. Experimental writing, customer-support and coding studies show gains in bounded settings, while other coding evidence finds slowdown; labour-market studies likewise range from short-term losses or reduced junior hiring to work reorganisation without adoption-driven declines. These are treated as differences in populations, horizons and identification strategies rather than one settled effect.

The voice materially develops the proposition in three ways. First, it identifies mechanisms—especially AI Interaction Competence, cognitive engagement and conceptual scaffolding—that help explain who benefits and how training can reduce dispersion. Second, randomized skill-formation evidence shows that assisted completion can impair later conceptual, code-reading and debugging performance, strengthening the distinction between throughput and learning and raising a prospective verification-capacity concern. Third, macroeconomic studies specify the assumptions required to move from task speed to labour-cost savings, aggregate growth, employment or welfare.

Material internal variation remains. Some studies find larger gains among novices, weaker performers or lower-education participants; others associate gains mainly with experienced or AI-skilled users. Some offer suggestive evidence of learning or immediate carryover, whereas another finds lower subsequent skill scores. Employment evidence includes reduced junior hiring and Upwork earnings losses, but also stable wages and hours and findings that observed declines were not driven by adopting firms. Aggregate-growth estimates are projections or model-based scenarios, not observed economy-wide outcomes. Thus, the sources broadly reinforce the cluster while extending it with mechanisms, interventions and explicit limits on aggregation; this characterisation applies only to the supplied curated sources, not academia or research generally.

qs.q: Our study complements this literature by providing controlled, causal micro-evidence: it isolates how differences in AIC levels shape productivity outcomes and demonstrates that lightweight process interventions—conceptual scaffolding and training—reduce variance without lowering mean performance.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: These curated legal-tech-vendor sources accept the proposition that measured task gains do not establish whole-job productivity, durable skill growth or broad economic effects. They collectively build on it by adding two complementary layers of evidence. The GitHub Copilot experiment demonstrates a substantial speed gain on one standardized programming task but limits generalization across tasks and leaves code quality and lasting skill formation untested. The Codex study moves beyond isolated tasks to delegated, multi-step agentic workflows and argues that realized value depends on organizational complements such as system access, workforce skills, workflow redesign, review and verification. Material internal variation lies mainly in method and emphasis: the Copilot source provides randomized task-level causal evidence, whereas the Codex source draws interpretive—not causal—organizational conclusions from differences in observed usage across user populations. Neither source shows that assisted performance produces durable learning or warrants worker-replacement claims.

qs.q: Productivity benefits may                                                    7 ^Lvary across specific tasks and programming languages, so more research is needed to understand how our results generalizes to other tasks.
qs.a: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot · Legal-tech vendor · 2023

qs.q: In this sense, agentic AI is not simply a cheaper input into existing work; its value depends on whether organizations can redesign workflows, responsibilities, and review processes around delega- tion and verification.
qs.a: The Shift to Agentic AI: Evidence from Codex · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: This market-analyst/research source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by showing why observed task-level productivity estimates cannot be generalized without accounting for actual usage, task selection and study participation. Developers increasingly withheld tasks they preferred to perform with AI, while highly enthusiastic adopters were also less likely to participate; the researchers therefore interpret their estimate as a likely lower bound, but appropriately stop short of treating preferences or missing observations as measured gains. This strengthens the cluster’s caution that adoption and perceived value are not substitutes for end-to-end evidence. Its scope is narrower than the full proposition: it addresses measurement bias in developer productivity rather than durable skill growth, whole-job effects, worker replacement or distributional outcomes. Because this facet contains one curated source, it establishes that source’s alignment, not the prevalence of this view among market analysts, consultancies or the press.

qs.q: -  **Developers have become more selective in which tasks they submit.** When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.
qs.a: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Together, these effects make it likely that our estimate reported above is a lower-bound on the true productivity effects of AI on these developers.
qs.a: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: Within this curated professional voice, the OECD supports the proposition’s distinction between demonstrated task-level performance gains and broader claims about productivity, replacement or durable skill growth. It synthesises early evidence of improved performance—often with larger gains for less-experienced or lower-skilled workers—and therefore aligns particularly strongly with the cluster’s equalisation finding. At the same time, it cautions that the studied applications are narrow and may not generalise across firms. Internal variation lies in who benefits: weaker writers may gain both speed and quality, stronger writers mainly speed, and survey results differ by education and occupation. The OECD does not directly test durable skill formation, whole-job productivity or worker replacement, so its support for those elements is limited rather than contradictory. As this facet contains one selected OECD source, it should not be treated as representative of regulators, courts and professional bodies generally.

qs.q: Emerging evidence shows that generative AI produces productivity gains and  equalises performance between workers in the same roles  Emerging research on the effect of generative AI applications in the workplace finds that they increase  productivity and often increase the performance of the least experienced or lowest skilled workers.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: worker productivity is consistent with emerging studies of adoption of generative AI applications in the workplace, although these applications tend to be quite specific in scope, and it is too soon to see how they generalise to a wider set of firms (see Box 4.2).
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source supports the proposition’s core distinction between AI assistance on particular programming tasks and broader claims about whole-job productivity or worker replacement. It presents benchmark performance and commercial deployment as reasons to investigate programmer–AI interaction, but frames the technology as an assistant working alongside programmers and asks which tasks programmers need help with. This is consistent with the cluster’s emphasis on task context and human contribution. The support is preliminary rather than conclusive: the excerpt relies on prior benchmark results, reports no study findings on end-to-end productivity, and provides no evidence about durable skill formation, experience effects, output quality, or employment. The main internal tension is between enthusiasm about model capabilities and a more cautious, task-centred research framing. Because this time-period facet contains only one curated source, no broader prevalence claim can be made.

qs.q: With this impressive performance, large code-generating models are quickly escaping research                                          labs to power industrial programming assistant tools, such as Github Copilot [Friedman 2021].
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

qs.q: The growing adoption of these tools gives rise to questions about the nature of AI-assisted                                          programming: What kinds of tasks do programmers need assistance with?
qs.a: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models · Academia · 2022

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that generative AI can produce substantial gains on bounded knowledge-work tasks without establishing uniform whole-job productivity, worker replacement or durable skill growth. Common reasons are that the strongest evidence comes from task-specific experiments; effects vary by task, baseline ability and experience; quality is not always measured or improved; and employment or aggregate-growth conclusions require assumptions beyond those experiments. Material variation concerns interpretation rather than the core distinction. Some sources frame AI as complementing expertise and narrowing performance gaps, especially for novices, while Noy and Zhang interpret writing gains mainly as substitution for effort rather than improvement in underlying skills. The Upwork study adds preliminary short-term evidence of reduced jobs and earnings among exposed freelancers, but explicitly does not settle longer-term displacement. Macroeconomic sources extend task findings into conditional labour-cost or growth estimates, while clearly treating them as modeled projections. Most sources do not directly test durable learning, so their support for the cluster’s skill-formation claim is principally that assisted performance should not be treated as evidence of lasting or transferable skill.

qs.q: Hence, from these experiments, we can only learn about the productivity gains, inclusive of any task complementarities—and not about the displacement effects.
qs.a: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: First, the tasks are relatively short, self-contained, and lack a dimension of context-specific knowledge, which may inflate our estimates of ChatGPT’s usefulness.
qs.a: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2023

elens.an:
The curated sources associated with 2025 support the proposition that AI’s effects on knowledge work are heterogeneous and that assisted task performance, whole-job productivity, durable skill formation and employment consequences must be evaluated separately. Their common reason is methodological as much as substantive: adoption, benchmark capability, output volume, perceived time savings and occupational exposure are not treated as interchangeable with measured end-to-end productivity or adoption-driven labour-market effects. Field and quasi-experimental evidence shows several distinct outcomes—performance gains in P&G product-development work, more coding and less project management among Copilot-eligible developers, and disproportionate benefits for some weaker or less-experienced workers—but these findings concern particular tasks, activity shares or worker groups and do not establish universal productivity gains, autonomous replacement or durable learning.

Material internal variation strengthens rather than undermines that conclusion. METR finds that experienced developers working in familiar, mature repositories took 19% longer with AI, despite believing they had become faster, whereas the P&G experiment reports substantial gains for AI-assisted individuals and continued human shaping of outputs. Labour-market findings are also contested: one firm-level study links deliberate GenAI adoption to reduced junior employment through slower hiring, while linked survey and administrative evidence finds stable wages and hours and reports that the examined employment declines were not driven by chatbot-adopting firms. Adoption research documents rapid diffusion but relatively low work-hour intensity and derives potential aggregate productivity from self-reported savings and modelling rather than direct measurement. Evidence on durable skill formation is notably thinner: the period’s sources mainly document immediate assistance, task reallocation and possible labour-market reorganisation, while explicitly limiting longer-run conclusions. This assessment describes the relationship of the curated sources to the proposition and does not imply that their views or findings represent all researchers or workplaces.

qs.q: We find that when developers use AI tools, they implement issues in 19% more time on average (Figure 1), and nearly all quantiles of observed implementation time see AI-allowed issues taking longer (Figure 5).

qs.q: Even as wages and recorded hours remain stable, workplaces adopt chatbot initiatives, workers take on new AI-related tasks, and adopters transition into new occupations.
qs.a: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects (revised as: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI) · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI-assisted task performance does not by itself establish whole-job productivity, worker replacement or durable skill growth. They materially develop it by identifying mechanisms and deployment conditions: AI Interaction Competence, cognitive engagement, targeted training, conceptual scaffolding, workflow redesign, system access, review and verification. Experimental evidence includes substantial but uneven task gains, education-gap compression, improved legal-analysis performance after instruction, and lower subsequent coding-skill scores after AI-assisted learning; observational and descriptive studies add evidence on experienced-user advantages, adoption patterns and early labour-market signals but appropriately stop short of causal claims. Material internal variation concerns who benefits: some experiments suggest larger gains for junior, lower-performing or lower-education participants, whereas observational coding evidence concentrates gains among experienced developers and competence-focused studies attribute returns to the ability to elicit, evaluate and verify outputs. Results also vary by task and institution, from positive coding-output effects to no significant speed gain during unfamiliar-skill acquisition and uncertainty about transfer to courts or broader firm activity. Thus, the period strengthens the proposition with concrete human-capital and organizational mechanisms, while leaving long-run deskilling, economy-wide productivity and employment effects unresolved.
